newsitem.title: USA: Brazil cenbank nominee inspires Wall St confidence.
newsitem.headline: Brazil cenbank nominee inspires Wall St confidence.

text.p: Wall Street analysts on Wednesday applauded the nomination of Gustavo Franco to head Brazil's central bank, and saw the move as solidifying the country's exchange rate policy.

U.S. analysts said they were impressed by Franco, named Tuesday to replace Gustavo Loyola, because of his commitment to economic stability, and the continued gradual devaluation of the nation's currency, the real.
Brazilian bond prices gained following the news.

"It's a strong reaffirmation of the commitment to the current economic progam and to the exchange rate regime," said Paulo Leme, senior international economist at Goldman Sachs. "Investors were reassured by that."
By midday Wednesday the liquid "C" bonds BR8D14=RR rose 2/8 to 84-5/8, while the country's global bond due 2027 climbed 3/4 to a 101 bid.

U.S. analysts commended the smooth manner in which Brazil handled the transition, which had been widely expected, given that Loyola had made known his desire to step down after implementing bank sector reform.
"There is a difference in style, but no difference in policy," Luis R. Luis, head of emerging market analysis at Scudder, Stevens & Clark said of the difference between Franco and Loyola.

Investors approved of the changing of the guard because of Franco's powerful reputation as archiect of the "real plan" that brought stability to an economy that was racked by hyperinflation three years ago.
John Welch, chief Latin America econmist at Paribas, said financial markets felt confident that Franco would use revenues from privatization to pay down some of the country's massive domestic debt.
"It erases some uncertainty about outside meddling, especially by those who would use privatization for other purposes," Welch said.

Welch said he did not expect any change in Brazil's exchange rate regime, in which the real is gradually devalued along a band system, until 1999. By then, he said, he expected the country would have made progress on fiscal refrorms.
A overhaul of the nation's fiscal system is seen as a key step for a long-term reduction of Brazil's domestic debt and the maintenance of investor's confidence in the real.
While investors saw Franco as highly capable, they said he faced major challenges, namely widening current account and trade imbalances.

"The challenges for Franco remain formidable as they try to engineer a soft landing from the build up of pressures in the external sector," Scudder's Luis said, adding the central bank needed Congress to approve key fiscal reforms.

"The central bank does not have all the tools to handle this," Luis said, adding that Franco will liekly need help from Finance Minister Pedro Malan and President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to ease pressures on the fiscal side.
